newsitem.title: USA: Dlr off slightly at U.S. noon, uninspired by Rubin.
newsitem.headline: Dlr off slightly at U.S. noon, uninspired by Rubin.

text.p: The dollar stood marginally weaker versus the yen at midday after remarks by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin failed to provide fresh direction for trading, according to currency experts.

Responding to questions after addressing a meeting of the Council for Electronic Revenue Communication Advancement, Rubin repeated that a sustained rise in Japan's trade surplus could hurt global growth and warned it could spark a protectionist backlash.
He reiterated that U.S. dollar policy remains unchanged and the U.S. will never use the dollar as a trade tool.

The flurry of comments from the Treasury Secretary also included the oft-made observation that excessive foreign exchange volatility is undesirable. But Rubin also said he was unsure if recent moves were excessive.
"He hasn't said anything he hasn't said before," said Diego Giurleo, a vice president of Treasury at Royal Bank of Canada.
Rubin was underscoring the fact that Japan's trade surplus position is unsustainable in the long run and the yen can not be used as a tool to generate surpluses, Guirleo said.
The dollar fetched 113.82/92 yen at midday, just shy of its opening level at 114.03/08. Shortly after midday, the greenback climbed back above 114 yen.
Some experts linked this dollar gain to trading in the crosses as well as the Rubin remarks.
"There seemed to be some activity in the mark/yen cross that seemed to help dollar/yen higher," said Joe Pedone, a vice president at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank.
Pedone also said there seemed to be short-covering of dollars for yen after the Rubin comments.
"As usual (Rubin) wasn't overly committal to either side," Pedone said.

"I don't know if the market really perceived his statements as being bullish for the dollar. It might have just been a timing thing and how the market was placed when the comments came out," Pedone added.

Earlier in the session, the dollar had pulled back slightly after the Commerce Department reported that retail sales fell 0.1 percent in May in both the overall measure and when car sales were left out. Economists expected, on average, for sales to rise 0.4 percent and 0.3 percent, respectively.

"(The data is) significant if it continues because we're starting to see the moderation in economic activity that the Federal Reserve has been expecting," said Brian McCarthy, a market analyst at Ruesch International.
However, the market has not seen the inflation indicators for May, which are expected to show that energy prices are not falling as quickly as earlier in the year, McCarthy said.
He said one of the reasons why the market has seen the paradox of low inflation and high economic growth is because energy prices have been artificially depressing the inflation rate.
On Friday, the Labor Department is scheduled to release the U.S. producer price index (PPI) for May at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
The May PPI is expected to rise 0.1 percent in both the overall measure and the core, which excludes volatile food and energy items, based on a Reuter poll.
In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.4405/15 Swiss francs from 1.4440/50, and to Canadian $1.3823/28 from C$1.3877/82.
The dollar was barely changed at 1.7243/48 marks compared with 1.7245/55 marks. The pound rose to $1.6350/60 from $1.6342/47. (( -- Donna Sells, 212-859-1668))
